subject: Restricting the range of positional vs non-positional scales

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Restricting the range of positional vs non-positional scales
parts:
I have a conceptual question about scales. Why is it that, if you restrict the range of x and y scales, the data points are removed, but if you restrict the range of other scales, the data points are NOT removed?

For example:

# Restrict color scale range: displays all 10 points
# Those outside color scale range are NA/gray
qplot(1:10,1:10, colour=1:10) + scale_colour_continuous(limits=c(3,7))

# Restrict x scale range (and zoom out using coord_cartesian):
#   displays only points from 3-7.
qplot(1:10,1:10, colour=1:10) + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(3,7)) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim=c(1,10))
# Warning message:
# Removed 5 rows containing missing values (geom_point). 


I guess it makes sense that if a point is outside of the x scale, it can't be displayed since its x position is literally off the scale. But why then should a point be drawn when its color is also off the scale?

-Winston

messages.author: affa918ed63b6275
messages.subject: Re: Restricting the range of positional vs non-positional scales
parts:
Hi,

Your question is probably relevant to my long-lasting consideration.

First, as you say, positional and non-positional scale is conceptually
different.
positional oob (out-of-bounds) values cannot be shown. na.values for
them doesn't make sense.
But non-positional oob values can be shown. na.values for them does make sense.

At the moment, I think, na.values makes some confusion.
Now oob values are substituted by NA.
However, NA already has a special meaning for data, i.e., "missing
value" usually.
Missing value and oob indicate definitely different things.

So finally I think oob and NA should be handled separately.
scale may have options `oob.value` and `na.value`
oob.value is either NA or omit. In the case of omit, oob values are
not displayed.
In the case of NA, oob values are displayed as if they are NA if possible.
Or oob.value may be some entity such as "red", "blue", to indicate the
data point is oob.

na.values specifies, say, actual color for color scale, size for size
scale, OR, omit.
If omit, NAs are not shown.

Probably these change will make things clear. What is important is to
handle NA and omit separately.

These are very rough picture though.

kohske

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Restricting the range of positional vs non-positional scales
parts:
To me, it doesn't seem like there should be a fundamental difference in positional (x, y) and non-positional (colour, fill, etc) scales. There's a practical difference, of course, but it seems to me that at an abstract level, they can be treated the same: each scale is essentially an axis in a multidimensional space.  

Just as it makes sense to do stat_summary(fun.y=mean), it also makes sense to do something like stat_summary(fun.colour=mean), even if this not very useful in practical terms. 

Positional scales are different for rendering, of course... but it's still unclear to me why data should get dropped completely in a positional scale but not in other scales. (I think there's a difference between dropping the data and simply not drawing it.)

Here's another way to illustrate the issue, with a stat that behaves differently depending on whether the data is dropped.

dat <- data.frame(x=1:10, y=c(1,1,1,9:12,20,20,20), col=1:10)

# Basic plot with lm line
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y, colour=col)) + geom_point() +
    stat_smooth(method=lm, se=FALSE)
p

# With smaller x range: 
#  data is dropped, so lm fits dots perfectly
p + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(4,7))
# Warning messages:
# 1: Removed 6 rows containing missing values (stat_smooth). 
# 2: Removed 6 rows containing missing values (geom_point). 

# With smaller color range:
#  data is not dropped, so lm is unchanged
p + scale_colour_continuous(limits=c(4,7))

# With smaller x scale and oob=rescale_none:
#  data is not dropped, so lm is unchanged
library(scales)
p + scale_x_continuous(limits=c(4,7), oob=rescale_none)


-Winston

Yes exactly. Absolutely there is no difference between P and NP (!) in

The difference only appears when they are rendered, in other words,
when we see them by our eyes.

>
> Just as it makes sense to do stat_summary(fun.y=mean), it also makes sense

I think that's useful anywhere to some extent.
Actually stat_summary2d is very similar to that.

> but not in other scales. (I think there's a difference between dropping the

That's consistent behavior. To make clear, I mean removing from stat
calculation by "drop."
So what is missing is, theoretically, the coord for NP scales.
But practically I don't feel coords for NP is necessary.

Basically there are two types of limits: limits for stat calculation
and limits for drawing.
So it would be good idea to make clear these points.

Hi Winston:

It seems to me that your examples are (at least superficially) related
to the issue of whether the data are transformed before statistics are
applied (in this case, the 'statistic' is the fitted line) or the
coordinate system is transformed after statistics are applied. I
haven't thought deeply about the oob construct, but perhaps some
checks are needed to ensure that it is applied consistently.

Instead of dropping data, one could censor it instead, but I don't

examples to get a feel for how NA, oob and censor behave and interact

alluded to above.

parts:
On Tue, Apr 24, 2012 at 3:44 PM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Winston:

It seems to me that your examples are (at least superficially) related
to the issue of whether the data are transformed before statistics are
applied (in this case, the 'statistic' is the fitted line) or the
coordinate system is transformed after statistics are applied. I
haven't thought deeply about the oob construct, but perhaps some
checks are needed to ensure that it is applied consistently.

I think you're right that they are related (see below).
 

...

Instead of dropping data, one could censor it instead, but I don't
know offhand what the implications would be. I'd have to try out some
examples to get a feel for how NA, oob and censor behave and interact
with one another in the composition of a graphic, and consider how the
result behaves wrt the data/coordinate transformation distinction
alluded to above.

Here's my understanding of what happens:

1. scale_x_continuous(), scale_colour_continuous(), and so on, all call continuous_scale().
2. In continuous_scale(), the default is oob=censor.
3. The censor() function (in scales) replaces any out-of-range values with NA.
4a. For scale_x_continuous, NAs are dropped (even if you set na.value).
4b. For scale_colour_continuous, NAs are replaced with na.value, which defaults to "grey50".
5. Stats are run.

At this point, it's a little less clear to me what happens, but I think that steps 3-4 happen again, so that for scale_x_continuous, out-of-range values are dropped, but for scale_colour_continuous, they're replaced with na.value.

-Winston

> To me, it doesn't seem like there should be a fundamental difference in

> level, they can be treated the same: each scale is essentially an axis in a

I don't think there should be either.

> Just as it makes sense to do stat_summary(fun.y=mean), it also makes sense
> to do something like stat_summary(fun.colour=mean), even if this not very
> useful in practical terms.
Agreed, but writing the function to make that work is complicated.

> Positional scales are different for rendering, of course... but it's still
> unclear to me why data should get dropped completely in a positional scale
> but not in other scales. (I think there's a difference between dropping the
> data and simply not drawing it.)

They did used to get dropped. I think Kohske correctly identifies the
problem: we are using NA is two different ways. If NA comes in the
original data, it should be displayed on the legend/axis. If it is
created because the data is outside the limits, it should be silently
dropped.

Hadley
